concept.name: Terminal value
concept.definition: The estimated value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast horizon in a DCF model, computed either as a growing perpetuity or as an exit multiple. It typically dominates the valuation, often contributing well over half of total present value.
concept.intuition: Since a business presumably outlives any five- or ten-year forecast, terminal value is the compressed answer to 'and then what?' - and where most of the value hides.
concept.mechanics: The Gordon-growth version sets TV = CF(n+1) / (r - g), with g capped at or below long-run nominal economic growth; the exit-multiple version applies an observed multiple such as EV/EBITDA to the final forecast year, which smuggles relative valuation into the DCF.
concept.formula: Terminal value = CF_(n+1) / (r - g); its present value is TV / (1+r)^n.
concept.failure_modes: The result explodes as g approaches r - a one-point change in either can double the value - and assuming g above long-run GDP growth implies the firm eventually grows larger than the economy itself.
concept.misconceptions: A large terminal-value share is not automatically a red flag - it is mathematically inevitable for growing firms - but it demands that growth and margin assumptions remain defensible far beyond the forecast window.
concept.example: In Damodaran's worked example, a firm whose five explicit years of equity cash flows total about $337 million carries a $1,603 million terminal value - roughly 80% of the present value of equity comes from beyond year five.

citations.source: Aswath Damodaran (NYU Stern), Discounted Cash Flow Valuation lecture notes
citations.section: Equity Valuation versus Firm Valuation: worked example
